GLOSSARY.definition: A separate, self-contained living space on the same property as a main home. Sometimes called a granny unit, in-law unit, backyard cottage, or second unit.
The official address assigned by the city or county for a new unit or building.
Whether the project is a detached ADU, attached ADU, or Junior ADU. The type affects which address, meter, and electrical-service questions need formal review.
A measure of electric current. Panel and main-breaker ratings are often shown in amps, such as 100A or 200A.
The city or county office responsible for permits and inspections for the project.
The required space around equipment so it is safe and accessible. Not meeting clearances can turn a project into a relocation.
The device that measures how much electricity the property uses. A meter is different from the electrical service connection and the electrical panel.
How much electricity the home or project needs when equipment is operating.
The breaker box that distributes electricity to circuits in a home or building. It contains the breakers, including the main breaker.
The connection that brings power from the utility to your property. Adding a meter does not always mean adding a service.
How much electrical power the current connection to the property can provide.
A scaled drawing of the outside wall of the building with the meter location marked.
The official utility application and review process. Project Navigator is before this step and does not start, submit, or approve anything.
A smaller unit created within the existing home. It is treated like an attached ADU only if it meets the complete-family-living-facilities test.
Replacing a panel with the same capacity, not increasing it. Going from under 100A to a new 100A is like-for-like, not an upgrade.
A licensed electrician's calculation of how much electrical power the property and planned equipment may need.
A form listing your equipment and expected power use, so the added load can be evaluated. Usually completed with a contractor or electrician.
The large switch in your panel that controls all power to the home. Its rating in amps tells you your panel size.
An electrical service path where visible wires typically reach the property from a pole.
The amount of electrical demand a panel is designed to carry. A load calculation and field review help determine whether the existing panel can support planned equipment.
The manufacturer specification sheet or a clear photo of the rating label that shows the panel's maximum rating.
Replacing a panel with a higher-capacity one so your service can carry more electricity.
Whether the ADU needs its own meter, its own service, or both. A meter is not the same as a service.
The wire that carries power from the utility line to your meter or panel.
A change to the electrical connection or capacity serving the property. It is not the same as replacing only the electrical panel.
A simple diagram showing how power flows from the service to your equipment. Usually prepared by an electrician.
A drawing or aerial view of your property showing where the meter is, with a north arrow and street names.
Common residential main-breaker ratings include 100, 125, 150, and 200 amps. A common size does not determine what a specific project needs.
An electrical service path that reaches the property below ground rather than through visible overhead wires.
A separate street address assigned by your city or county, sometimes required before a second meter or service can be set.
